[THOUGHT] The skin examination finding — “three 2–3 mm, dome-shaped, hardened papules on the left thigh with central umbilication” — is highly specific. Central umbilication is the hallmark of **molluscum contagiosum**, a poxvirus infection. While the patient previously denied a “pearly or waxy appearance”, umbilication is distinct and more definitive; it may have been overlooked or not described in lay terms. The size (2–3 mm), number (three), hardness, and location align perfectly with molluscum. This finding discriminates strongly against verruca plana (which lacks umbilication and is flat-topped), dermatofibroma (no umbilication, usually solitary, dimpling on lateral pressure—not umbilication), and melanocytic nevus (no umbilication, soft to firm, no central depression). Molluscum is common in adults via close contact (including sexual or non-sexual skin-to-skin), often asymptomatic, and persists for weeks to months — matching the 3-week timeline. No further testing is needed: the physical exam finding is diagnostic.

[DIAGNOSIS] Molluscum contagiosum

[THOUGHT]  
The new clinical information — obtained at turn 9 — is highly specific and diagnostically decisive:  
- **Three lesions**, each **2–3 mm**, **dome-shaped**, **hardened**, and with **central umbilication**.  
- “Umbilication” (a central dimple or depression) is a *pathognomonic* clinical feature of **molluscum contagiosum**, especially when combined with:  
  • Small size (2–5 mm),  
  • Dome-shaped, pearly or waxy (though patient previously denied “pearly/waxy” — possibly due to subtle presentation or recall limitation),  
  • Firmness/hardness (consistent with viral inclusion bodies in keratinocytes),  
  • Absence of inflammation, pruritus, or pain (typical of early/mild molluscum).  
- The number (three) fits the common presentation — not solitary (arguing against dermatofibroma or intradermal nevus), not numerous (making flat warts less likely, though possible), and clustered on one site (favoring autoinoculation).  
- All other considered entities are now strongly disfavored:  
  • *Dermatofibroma*: Typically solitary, tethered, with dimple sign *on lateral squeeze*, not inherent umbilication; no umbilication reported histologically or clinically in classic cases.  
  • *Intradermal melanocytic nevus*: Soft, non-umbilicated, rarely multiple in same small area without other nevi; no association with umbilication.  
  • *Seborrheic keratosis*: Uncommon on thigh, larger, “stuck-on”, verrucous — inconsistent with 2–3 mm dome-shaped umbilicated papules.  

Thus, the physical exam finding at turn 9 provides sufficient objective evidence for a confident clinical diagnosis — *without requiring histopathology*.

[SUMMARY]  
**Diagnosis:** **Molluscum contagiosum** (clinically confirmed).  

**Key Diagnostic Features (from Turn 9 Skin Exam):**  
- **Number & Distribution:** Three discrete papules on the left thigh — consistent with localized, self-inoculated spread.  
- **Morphology:**  
  • Size: 2–3 mm (classic range for molluscum),  
  • Shape: Dome-shaped,  
  • Surface: Central umbilication (pathognomonic),
